title: Objective Measures and Candidate Biomarkers for Deep Brain Stimulation in Pediatric Dystonia: A Scoping Review
content: Objective: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can provide clinically meaningful improvement for children with medically refractory dystonia, but response is heterogeneous and programming is often prolonged. We reviewed imaging, neurophysiological, and quantitative movement measures that may improve candidate assessment, programming, longitudinal monitoring, and personalized DBS care. Methods: We conducted a scoping review using established Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported it in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through August 27, 2026. Evidence was organized around four clinical questions and separated into reports involving DBS care and non-DBS pediatric dystonia studies evaluating objective measures potentially applicable to DBS follow-up. Results: Sixty-one reports were included: 38 evaluated objective measures within a DBS-care context, and 23 evaluated quantitative measures in non-DBS pediatric dystonia cohorts. DBS-context studies addressed preoperative imaging and physiology, programming and target engagement, chronic sensing, actigraphy/accelerometry, quantitative follow-up, and individualized targeting. Non-DBS studies evaluated gait, upper-limb kinematics, electromyography, coherence, and markerless video measures. Across overlapping evidence categories, 19 reports were case reports or small series, 17 used retrospective association or modeling, and 41 included prospective or protocolized evaluation; two included an external-validation analysis, and none formally tested incremental clinical utility beyond standard care. Conclusions: Pediatric DBS biomarker research is moving from descriptive physiology toward clinically relevant tools for prediction, programming, and longitudinal monitoring. The next steps are prospective multisite studies using standardized acquisition and clinically meaningful outcomes to determine whether objective measures improve decisions or reduce burden beyond experienced multidisciplinary care.
